claim: Vibrissa sensory inputs play a central role in driving rodent behavior.

claim: Vibrissa sensory inputs transit through the sensory trigeminal nuclei.

evidence: This statement draws from established knowledge about the vibrissa sensory pathway.

claim: The sensory trigeminal nuclei give rise to the ascending lemniscal and paralemniscal pathways.

claim: Lemniscal projections are somatotopically mapped from brainstem to cortex.

claim: Paralemniscal pathway projections are more widely distributed than lemniscal projections.

claim: The extent and topography of paralemniscal projections are unknown.

claim: The paralemniscal pathway broadcasts vibrissa-based sensory signals to brainstem regions involved in the regulation of autonomic functions.

claim: Most sensory systems comprise parallel pathways of sensory information that encode different features of a stimulus.

claim: The lemniscal pathway arises from the trigeminal nucleus principalis (PrV).

evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to a review article.

claim: KF/PBc cells that receive interpolaris input project to the lateral part of the bed nucleus of stria terminalis.
source: Ascending projections were found in the dorsal raphe, the Edinger-Wesphal nucleus, the periaqueductal gray, the posterior lateral hypothalamus, the paracentral and central medial thalamic nuclei, the parvicellular part of the ventral posterior thalamic nucleus, the ventral division of zona incerta, the central amygdala (CeA), and the lateral part of the bed nucleus of stria terminalis in all animals (Figure 2E–G - Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is a finding of the current study based on transsynaptic tracing experiments shown in Figure 2E-G and Figure 2—figure supplement 1.

claim: KF/PBc cells that receive interpolaris input project to most of the brainstem and forebrain regions previously identified by means of anterograde tracer injections in the KF/PBc.
source: In summary, KF/PBc cells that receive interpolaris input in turn project to most of the brainstem and forebrain regions previously identified by means of anterograde tracer injections in the KF/PBc (Saper and Stornetta, 2015; Figure 2H).
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the current study's data and comparison with prior literature.

claim: No anterograde labeling is observed in the trigeminal sensory nuclei from KF/PBc cells that receive interpolaris input.
source: Yet, it is worth noting that no anterograde labeling is observed in the trigeminal sensory nuclei.
evidence: This is a finding of the current study based on transsynaptic tracing experiments.

claim: KF/PBc cells that receive interpolaris input do not feedback to the relay cells that give rise to the paralemniscal pathway.
source: This negative result is of critical importance. It indicates that KF/PBc cells that receive interpolaris input do not feedback to the relay cells that give rise to the paralemniscal pathway (see below).
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the absence of anterograde labeling in the trigeminal sensory nuclei.

claim: Prior studies in mice have shown that separate pools of KF/PBc neurons project to the forebrain and to the lower brainstem.
source: Prior studies in mice have shown that separate pools of KF/PBc neurons project to the forebrain and to the lower brainstem (Geerling et al., 2017; Barik et al., 2018).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: Vibrissa deflection evoked a clear negative field potential in the CeA with a peak latency of 12 ms.
source: Vibrissa deflection evoked a clear negative field potential in the CeA (peak latency of 12 ms as an average over all three rats and 50 trials per rat; Figure 3A and B).
evidence: This is a finding of the current study based on electrophysiological recordings shown in Figure 3A-B.

claim: The vibrissa-evoked response in the CeA was abolished following electrolytic lesion of the ipsilateral PB nucleus.
source: This response was abolished in all animals following electrolytic lesion of the ipsilateral PB nucleus (Figure 3A and C).
evidence: This is a finding of the current study based on electrophysiological recordings and lesion experiments shown in Figure 3A and C.

claim: Amygdala-projecting cells were concentrated in lateral and medial PB nucleus.
source: In detail, amygdala-projecting cells (326 in rat 1 and 312 in rat 2) were concentrated in lateral and medial PB nucleus, while the majority of facial projecting cells (299 in rat 1 and 140 in rat 2) were located in KF nucleus.
evidence: This is a finding of the current study based on retrograde tracing experiments.

claim: The majority of facial projecting cells were located in KF nucleus.
source: In detail, amygdala-projecting cells (326 in rat 1 and 312 in rat 2) were concentrated in lateral and medial PB nucleus, while the majority of facial projecting cells (299 in rat 1 and 140 in rat 2) were located in KF nucleus.
evidence: This is a finding of the current study based on retrograde tracing experiments.

claim: None of the KF/PBc cells were doubly labeled for projections to both the CeA and the facial nucleus.
source: Although a number of retrogradely labeled cells were found in the KF/PBc, none was doubly labeled.
evidence: This is a finding of the current study based on retrograde tracing experiments.

claim: Neighboring but separate populations of KF/PBc neurons project to the forebrain and to the lower brainstem.
source: Taken together, these results confirm that neighboring but separate populations of KF/PBc neurons project to the forebrain and to the lower brainstem (Figure 3H).
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the current study's data and comparison with prior literature.

claim: In rodents, KF projections to the brainstem arise from two neuronal populations: glutamatergic cells that project to the autonomic, respiratory, and motor regions of the medulla, and GABAergic neurons, which project principally to subnucleus SpVI.
source: In rodents, KF projections to the brainstem arise from two neuronal populations: glutamatergic cells that project to the autonomic, respiratory, and motor regions of the medulla, and GABAergic neurons, which project principally to subnucleus SpVI (Geerling et al., 2017).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to prior literature.

claim: Few interpolaris neurons were labeled by transsynaptic tracing from the KF/PBc.
source: Unexpectedly, few interpolaris neurons were labeled (44, 48, and 53 cells, respectively, in each of three rats).
evidence: This is a finding of the current study based on transsynaptic tracing experiments.

claim: Anterograde labeling from transsynaptic tracing from the KF/PBc was observed in the KF/PBc.
source: Anterograde labeling was observed in the KF/PBc and in the parvicellular part of the ventral posterior thalamic nucleus, a region known to process input from the tongue and oral cavity (Ogawa and Nomura, 1988; Verhagen et al., 2003), in all animals.
evidence: This is a finding of the current study based on transsynaptic tracing experiments.

claim: Anterograde labeling from transsynaptic tracing from the KF/PBc was observed in the parvicellular part of the ventral posterior thalamic nucleus.
source: Anterograde labeling was observed in the KF/PBc and in the parvicellular part of the ventral posterior thalamic nucleus, a region known to process input from the tongue and oral cavity (Ogawa and Nomura, 1988; Verhagen et al., 2003), in all animals.
evidence: This is a finding of the current study based on transsynaptic tracing experiments.

claim: The parvicellular part of the ventral posterior thalamic nucleus is a region known to process input from the tongue and oral cavity.
source: Anterograde labeling was observed in the KF/PBc and in the parvicellular part of the ventral posterior thalamic nucleus, a region known to process input from the tongue and oral cavity (Ogawa and Nomura, 1988; Verhagen et al., 2003), in all animals.
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: No labeling was observed in the cerebellum from transsynaptic tracing from the KF/PBc.
source: No labeling was observed in the cerebellum, nor in brainstem and midbrain regions that receive input from the paralemniscal pathway (Figure 2H).
evidence: This is a finding of the current study based on transsynaptic tracing experiments.

claim: No labeling was observed in brainstem and midbrain regions that receive input from the paralemniscal pathway from transsynaptic tracing from the KF/PBc.
source: No labeling was observed in the cerebellum, nor in brainstem and midbrain regions that receive input from the paralemniscal pathway (Figure 2H).
evidence: This is a finding of the current study based on transsynaptic tracing experiments.

claim: Cells in the parvicellular reticular formation (PCRt) at the medial border of the trigeminal nuclei were extensively labeled by transsynaptic tracing from the KF/PBc.
source: Yet, cells in the parvicellular reticular formation (PCRt) at the medial border of the trigeminal nuclei were extensively labeled, which indicates that the paucity of cell labeling in subnucleus SpVI is hardly ascribable to a technical pitfall.
evidence: This is a finding of the current study based on transsynaptic tracing experiments.

claim: KF projections do not innervate the SpVI interneurons or the projection cells that give rise to the paralemniscal pathway.
source: Taken together, these results indicate that KF projections do not innervate the SpVI interneurons or the projection cells that give rise to the paralemniscal pathway.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the transsynaptic tracing experiments.

claim: Optogenetic stimulation suppressed sensory-evoked discharges in monovibrissa-responsive cells.
source: Optogenetic stimulation suppressed sensory-evoked discharges in monovibrissa-responsive cells (26 cells in the same three rats, t-test yields p<0.001; lower panel in Figure 4G) but did not affect the firing of multivibrissa-responsive units (32 cells in the same three rats, p=0.84; Figure 4G).
evidence: This is a finding of the current study based on optogenetic experiments shown in Figure 4G.

claim: Optogenetic stimulation did not affect the firing of multivibrissa-responsive units.
source: Optogenetic stimulation suppressed sensory-evoked discharges in monovibrissa-responsive cells (26 cells in the same three rats, t-test yields p<0.001; lower panel in Figure 4G) but did not affect the firing of multivibrissa-responsive units (32 cells in the same three rats, p=0.84; Figure 4G).
evidence: This is a finding of the current study based on optogenetic experiments shown in Figure 4G.

claim: KF-induced suppression of sensory responses in local circuit interpolaris cells is mediated by presynaptic or extrasynaptic inhibition.
source: Together with the lack of transsynaptic labeling of local circuit cells from the KF nucleus, these results raise the possibility that KF-induced suppression of sensory responses in local circuit interpolaris cells is mediated by presynaptic or extrasynaptic inhibition, as summarized in Figure 4H.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the optogenetic and anatomical experiments, presented as a possibility.

claim: The most abundant collateral projection of vibrissa-responsive interpolaris cells is to the MdD nucleus and the dorsal horn of the cervical cord.
source: By far the most abundant collateral projection of vibrissa-responsive interpolaris cells is to the MdD nucleus and the dorsal horn of the cervical cord.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the anatomical data presented in the study.

claim: The finding of vibrissa-responsive cells in the MdD nucleus is unexpected.
source: The finding of vibrissa-responsive cells in the MdD nucleus is unexpected, as most studies reported that MdD neurons best respond to noxious stimuli (reviewed in Martins and Tavares, 2017; Figure 3A–C).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to a review article and comparison with the current study's data.

claim: Most studies reported that MdD neurons best respond to noxious stimuli.
source: The finding of vibrissa-responsive cells in the MdD nucleus is unexpected, as most studies reported that MdD neurons best respond to noxious stimuli (reviewed in Martins and Tavares, 2017; Figure 3A–C).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to a review article.

claim: An unexpected air puff directed toward the head of a rat elicits fear-related behavior such as a startle response.
source: Although there is no reason to believe that vibrissa deflection per se is painful, an unexpected air puff directed toward the head of a rat elicits fear-related behavior such as a startle response (Engelmann et al., 1996), 22 kHz ultrasonic vocalization (Knapp and Pohorecky, 1995), and avoidance behavior (Cimadevilla et al., 2001).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: An unexpected air puff directed toward the head of a rat elicits 22 kHz ultrasonic vocalization.
source: Although there is no reason to believe that vibrissa deflection per se is painful, an unexpected air puff directed toward the head of a rat elicits fear-related behavior such as a startle response (Engelmann et al., 1996), 22 kHz ultrasonic vocalization (Knapp and Pohorecky, 1995), and avoidance behavior (Cimadevilla et al., 2001).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: An unexpected air puff directed toward the head of a rat elicits avoidance behavior.
source: Although there is no reason to believe that vibrissa deflection per se is painful, an unexpected air puff directed toward the head of a rat elicits fear-related behavior such as a startle response (Engelmann et al., 1996), 22 kHz ultrasonic vocalization (Knapp and Pohorecky, 1995), and avoidance behavior (Cimadevilla et al., 2001).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: The MdD nucleus sends profuse projections to the cervical cord and the facial nucleus.
source: As the MdD nucleus sends profuse projections to the cervical cord and the facial nucleus (Bernard et al., 1990; Takatoh et al., 2013; Takatoh et al., 2021), these results suggest that vibrissa messages to the MdD nucleus may elicit avoidance or flight behaviors.
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: Vibrissa messages to the MdD nucleus may elicit avoidance or flight behaviors.
source: As the MdD nucleus sends profuse projections to the cervical cord and the facial nucleus (Bernard et al., 1990; Takatoh et al., 2013; Takatoh et al., 2021), these results suggest that vibrissa messages to the MdD nucleus may elicit avoidance or flight behaviors.
evidence: This is a speculation based on the anatomical data and prior literature.

claim: The MdD nucleus is part of a brainstem-spinal circuit to control escape responses to noxious stimuli.
source: This conclusion is in line with that of the recent study, which reported that the MdD nucleus is part of a brainstem-spinal circuit to control escape responses to noxious stimuli (Barik et al., 2018).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to prior literature.

claim: The brainstem medullary reticular formation comprises two main divisions: a ventral part (MdV) and a dorsal part (MdD).
source: The brainstem medullary reticular formation comprises two main divisions: a ventral part (MdV) and a dorsal part (MdD).
evidence: This statement draws from established knowledge about the anatomy of the medullary reticular formation.

claim: The MDV nucleus specifically targets subpopulations of forelimb-innervating motor neurons.
source: The MDV nucleus stands out as specifically targeting subpopulations of forelimb-innervating motor neurons.
evidence: This statement draws from established knowledge about the function of the MdV nucleus.

claim: Selective ablation or silencing experiments reveal that the MdV nucleus is critically important for skilled motor behaviors.
source: Selective ablation or silencing experiments reveal that the MdV nucleus is critically important for skilled motor behaviors (Esposito et al., 2014).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to prior literature.

claim: The MdD nucleus receives parabrachial inputs whose activation induces flight and escape behavior.
source: On the other hand, the MdD nucleus receives parabrachial inputs whose activation induces flight and escape behavior.
evidence: This statement draws from established knowledge about the function of the MdD nucleus.

claim: Activation of PB(tac1) neurons does not produce nocifensive responses on its own but has a major effect on responses to sensory cues.
source: Yet 'Activation of PB(tac1) neurons does not produce nocifensive responses on its own but has a major effect on responses to sensory cues. It thus seems possible that peripheral inputs provide the context necessary to trigger a specific behavioral response'. (Barik et al., 2018).
evidence: This statement is a direct quote from a prior study.

claim: The relay of sensory signals in the paralemniscal pathway is normally gated, and release from gating occurs in behavioral contexts that are alarming or threatening.
source: We propose that the relay of sensory signals in the paralemniscal pathway is normally gated, and that release from gating occurs in behavioral contexts that are alarming or threatening.
evidence: This is a proposal based on the current study's data and prior literature.

claim: GABAergic KF/PBc cells gate the relay of aversive stimuli to limbic forebrain regions.
source: A recent paper (Sun et al., 2020) lends support for this proposal by showing that GABAergic KF/PBc cells gate the relay of aversive stimuli to limbic forebrain regions.
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to prior literature.

claim: A number of studies have reported trigeminal projections to the KF and PB nuclei.
source: A number of studies have reported trigeminal projections to the KF and PB nuclei (Cechetto et al., 1985; Slugg and Light, 1994; Feil and Herbert, 1995; Dallel et al., 2004; Rodriguez et al., 2017; see also review by Chamberlin, 2004).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: Most studies on trigeminal projections to the KF and PB nuclei focused on ascending projections from subnucleus caudalis.
source: Most of these studies focused on ascending projections from subnucleus caudalis, which convey pruriceptive and nociceptive inputs to the KF/PBc (Jansen and Giesler, 2015).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: Subnucleus caudalis conveys pruriceptive and nociceptive inputs to the KF/PBc.
source: Most of these studies focused on ascending projections from subnucleus caudalis, which convey pruriceptive and nociceptive inputs to the KF/PBc (Jansen and Giesler, 2015).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to prior literature.

claim: One study previously reported short-latency activation of amygdala neurons, at about 11 ms, upon electrical stimulation of the mystacial pad.
source: One study previously reported short-latency activation of amygdala neurons, at about 11 ms, upon electrical stimulation of the mystacial pad (Bernard et al., 1992).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to prior literature.

claim: A short latency of about 11 ms for amygdala activation is consistent with the activation of a trigemino-parabrachial-amygdaloid pathway by Aβ primary vibrissa afferents.
source: Such a short latency is consistent with the activation of a trigemino-parabrachial-amygdaloid pathway by Aβ primary vibrissa afferents.
evidence: This is an inference based on the latency data from prior literature.

claim: Vibrissa-responsive interpolaris cells do not respond to noxious stimuli.
source: Although vibrissa-responsive interpolaris cells do not respond to noxious stimuli, many of the regions they innervate contain cells that process nociceptive or aversive inputs.
evidence: This statement draws from established knowledge about interpolaris cells.

claim: Many of the regions innervated by vibrissa-responsive interpolaris cells contain cells that process nociceptive or aversive inputs.
source: Although vibrissa-responsive interpolaris cells do not respond to noxious stimuli, many of the regions they innervate contain cells that process nociceptive or aversive inputs.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the anatomical data and prior literature.

claim: The MdD nucleus contains cells that process nociceptive or aversive inputs.
source: This is the case for the MdD nucleus (reviewed in Martins and Tavares, 2017), the KF/PBc (Jansen and Giesler, 2015), the superior colliculus (Dean et al., 1989; Redgrave et al., 1996), the zona incerta (Masri et al., 2009), and Po thalamus (Masri et al., 2009; Frangeul et al., 2014; Sobolewski et al., 2015).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to a review article.

claim: The KF/PBc contains cells that process nociceptive or aversive inputs.
source: This is the case for the MdD nucleus (reviewed in Martins and Tavares, 2017), the KF/PBc (Jansen and Giesler, 2015), the superior colliculus (Dean et al., 1989; Redgrave et al., 1996), the zona incerta (Masri et al., 2009), and Po thalamus (Masri et al., 2009; Frangeul et al., 2014; Sobolewski et al., 2015).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to prior literature.

claim: The superior colliculus contains cells that process nociceptive or aversive inputs.
source: This is the case for the MdD nucleus (reviewed in Martins and Tavares, 2017), the KF/PBc (Jansen and Giesler, 2015), the superior colliculus (Dean et al., 1989; Redgrave et al., 1996), the zona incerta (Masri et al., 2009), and Po thalamus (Masri et al., 2009; Frangeul et al., 2014; Sobolewski et al., 2015).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: The zona incerta contains cells that process nociceptive or aversive inputs.
source: This is the case for the MdD nucleus (reviewed in Martins and Tavares, 2017), the KF/PBc (Jansen and Giesler, 2015), the superior colliculus (Dean et al., 1989; Redgrave et al., 1996), the zona incerta (Masri et al., 2009), and Po thalamus (Masri et al., 2009; Frangeul et al., 2014; Sobolewski et al., 2015).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to prior literature.

claim: Po thalamus contains cells that process nociceptive or aversive inputs.
source: This is the case for the MdD nucleus (reviewed in Martins and Tavares, 2017), the KF/PBc (Jansen and Giesler, 2015), the superior colliculus (Dean et al., 1989; Redgrave et al., 1996), the zona incerta (Masri et al., 2009), and Po thalamus (Masri et al., 2009; Frangeul et al., 2014; Sobolewski et al., 2015).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: The paralemniscal pathway conveys signals from threatening or alarming sensory inputs, perhaps through association with aversive contexts.
source: These anatomical data suggest that the paralemniscal pathway conveys signals from threatening or alarming sensory inputs, perhaps through association with aversive contexts.
evidence: This is a speculation based on the anatomical data.

claim: The KF nucleus is primarily involved in orchestrating defensive reactions to aversive and threatening stimuli.
source: In light of the evidence that interpolaris cells innervate brain regions that process nociceptive or aversive stimuli, we postulate that the KF nucleus is primarily involved in orchestrating defensive reactions to aversive and threatening stimuli.
evidence: This is a postulate based on the current study's data and prior literature.

claim: Glutamatergic KF cells project to the cardio-respiratory medullary centers, the facial, hypoglossal, and ambiguous motor nuclei, the nucleus of the solitary tract, and to the preganglionic neurons of the sympathetic nervous systems.
source: First, glutamatergic KF cells project to the cardio-respiratory medullary centers, the facial, hypoglossal, and ambiguous motor nuclei, the nucleus of the solitary tract, and to the preganglionic neurons of the sympathetic nervous systems (reviewed in Saper and Stornetta, 2015).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to a review article.

claim: Activation of KF cells elicits changes in respiration, heart rate, blood pressure.
source: Second, activation of KF cells elicits changes in respiration, heart rate, blood pressure (Chamberlin and Saper, 1992; Lara et al., 1994; Guo et al., 2002; Chamberlin, 2004).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: Individual KF neurons project to many targets by means of branching axons.
source: Third, individual KF neurons project to many of the above-mentioned targets by means of branching axons, which might form the anatomical substrate for coordinating autonomic and somatic reactions (Song et al., 2012).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to prior literature.

claim: Branching axons of individual KF neurons might form the anatomical substrate for coordinating autonomic and somatic reactions.
source: Third, individual KF neurons project to many of the above-mentioned targets by means of branching axons, which might form the anatomical substrate for coordinating autonomic and somatic reactions (Song et al., 2012).
evidence: This is a speculation based on the anatomical data from prior literature.

claim: Units in trigeminal nucleus principalis fire more spikes when the animal is whisking as opposed to not whisking.
source: A prior study in the alert head-restrained rat reported that units in trigeminal nucleus principalis fire more spikes when the animal is whisking as opposed to not whisking (Moore et al., 2015).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to prior literature.

claim: Spike rates are not significantly different between whisking and not whisking in subnucleus SpVI.
source: Yet the same study shows that spike rates are not significantly different between whisking and not whisking in subnucleus SpVI.
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to prior literature.

claim: Primary vibrissa afferents discharge during whisking.
source: This is an unexpected result, as primary vibrissa afferents discharge during whisking (Severson et al., 2017) and SpVI projection cells are typically driven by many more vibrissae than principalis neurons (Furuta et al., 2006).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to prior literature.

claim: SpVI projection cells are typically driven by many more vibrissae than principalis neurons.
source: This is an unexpected result, as primary vibrissa afferents discharge during whisking (Severson et al., 2017) and SpVI projection cells are typically driven by many more vibrissae than principalis neurons (Furuta et al., 2006).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to prior literature.

claim: Whisking tends to reorganize spike times of neurons in interpolaris, rather than increase overall spike rates.
source: The observation that whisking tends to reorganize spike times of neurons in interpolaris, rather than increase overall spike rates, supports the notion that the relay of vibrissa messages in the paralemniscal pathway is normally gated as part of fast, inhibitory feedback.
evidence: This statement draws from prior literature and supports a conclusion about gating in the paralemniscal pathway.

claim: The relay of vibrissa messages in the paralemniscal pathway is normally gated as part of fast, inhibitory feedback.
source: The observation that whisking tends to reorganize spike times of neurons in interpolaris, rather than increase overall spike rates, supports the notion that the relay of vibrissa messages in the paralemniscal pathway is normally gated as part of fast, inhibitory feedback.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on prior literature and the current study's data.

claim: The KF nucleus receives projections from different subdivisions of the periaqueductal gray.
source: The KF nucleus receives projections from different subdivisions of the periaqueductal gray, themselves downstream of inhibitory input from the amygdala (Tovote et al., 2016).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to prior literature.

claim: The periaqueductal gray is downstream of inhibitory input from the amygdala.
source: The KF nucleus receives projections from different subdivisions of the periaqueductal gray, themselves downstream of inhibitory input from the amygdala (Tovote et al., 2016).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to prior literature.

claim: The release of the inhibition from the amygdala to the periaqueductal gray may lead to defensive postures.
source: The release of the inhibition from the amygdala to the periaqueductal gray may well lead to a defensive postures.
evidence: This is a speculation based on prior literature.

claim: Release of inhibition provides a release from pain.
source: It is of interest the release of inhibition provides a release from pain (Benarroch, 2012), also consistent with presynaptic inhibition of the trigeminus.
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to prior literature.

claim: The Kölliker-Fuse nucleus is currently considered to control the mechanics of respiratory and cardiac rhythms.
source: They provide a different viewpoint on the role of the Kölliker-Fuse nucleus, which is currently considered to control the mechanics of respiratory and cardiac rhythms, but no more.
evidence: This statement draws from established knowledge about the KF nucleus.

claim: The Kölliker-Fuse nucleus is involved in the larger role of orchestrating the expression of emotional reactions, for example, facial expressions, autonomic, and somatic reactions, of which respiration is one of many players.
source: We propose that the Kölliker-Fuse nucleus is involved in the larger role of orchestrating the expression of emotional reactions, for example, facial expressions, autonomic, and somatic reactions, of which respiration is one of many players.
evidence: This is a proposal based on the current study's data and prior literature.

claim: Experiments were carried out in Long Evans rats of both sexes and included five juvenile rats (P30–P35) and 36 adult rats (P80–P100; 250–350 g in mass).
source: Experiments were carried out in Long Evans rats of both sexes and included five juvenile rats (P30–P35) and 36 adult rats (P80–P100; 250–350 g in mass).
evidence: This is a description of the experimental subjects used in the study.

claim: All experiments were carried out according to the National Institutes of Health Guidelines.
source: All experiments were carried out according to the National Institutes of Health Guidelines.
evidence: This is a statement about the ethical conduct of the experiments.

claim: All experiments were approved by the Institutional Animal Care and Use Committees at Laval University and at the University of California at San Diego.
source: All experiments were approved by the Institutional Animal Care and Use Committees at Laval University and at the University of California at San Diego.
evidence: This is a statement about the ethical approval of the experiments.

claim: Different populations of SpVI cells project to the thalamus and cerebellum.
source: This is consistent with prior studies, which reported that different populations of SpVI cells project to the thalamus and cerebellum (Steindler, 1985; Jacquin et al., 1986).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: In sagittal sections of the brainstem, the terminal field of interpolaris axons in the KF/PBc covers an extensive crescent-shaped territory at the rostral border of the PrV and trigeminal motor nuclei.
source: Of note, in sagittal sections of the brainstem, the terminal field of interpolaris axons in the KF/PBc covers an extensive crescent-shaped territory at the rostral border of the PrV and trigeminal motor nuclei (Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is a finding of the current study based on anatomical data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claim: α2 agonists, for example, xylazine, strongly depress synaptic transmission in the parabrachial-amygdaloid pathway.
source: These experiments were carried out under urethane instead of ketamine/xylazine anesthesia as α2 agonists, for example, xylazine, strongly depress synaptic transmission in the parabrachial-amygdaloid pathway (Delaney et al., 2007).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to prior literature.
